status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating 'The authors show with very precise lesions that when the MB connections with the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden (VTNg) or the connections of the ascending mammillothalamic tract (MMT) to the anterior thalamus are eliminated, large deficits in spatial memory occur.' They describe these as 'interesting and important results' and note the 'remarkable finding' regarding maze rotation effects, indicating acceptance of the behavioral impairments in MTTx and VTNx groups.

Reviewers acknowledge that 'elimination of connections provided by the postcommissural fornix (PCF) have little effect' but express concern about interpretation, stating 'In a more classical view of these structures, the lack of effect of PCF lesions can be considered surprising. What then is the role of the PCF?' They request 'more detailed, explicit discussion of their ideas on this' to clarify the dissociation of memory systems, indicating uncertainty about the functional implications of these null findings.

Reviewers note that 'The effects on behaviour were correlated with reduced c-Fos expression in the retrosplenial cortex, the hippocampal formation, and the prelimbic cortex' but express caution, stating 'It may well be that these reductions are the direct consequences of the lesions. On the other hand, the situation is likely to be rather complicated and other pathways could also be directly or indirectly involved.' This indicates acceptance of the c-Fos reductions as observed but uncertainty about their mechanistic interpretation.

Reviewers question the anatomical characterization, stating 'the authors note that the mammillary body is reduced in size (atrophied) as a result of PCFx and they attribute this to loss of white matter. However, it is difficult to determine this from Figure 1G,H.' They request 'Improved photomicrographs' and suggest 'some measurements of the neurons might further substantiate this conclusion,' indicating that while the size reduction is acknowledged, the interpretation regarding white matter loss versus neuronal changes requires better evidence.

Reviewers ask 'do MMT or VTNg lesions have no effect on MB neurons?' in the context of requesting more detailed anatomical analyses. This question indicates uncertainty about the claim that reduced cross-sectional area combined with unchanged cell packing reflects cell loss in MTTx and VTNx groups, as reviewers seek additional measurements to substantiate this interpretation.

Reviewers specifically critique the hippocampal c-Fos analysis, stating 'The hippocampus (e.g., hippocampus and dentate gyrus) are lumped together but no mention is made of, nor illustrations provided of, which neurons and layer are or are not c-Fos positive.' This indicates that while the overall hippocampal c-Fos reduction may be accepted, the claim that changes are 'largely driven by reductions in CA1' requires more detailed anatomical documentation.

While reviewers acknowledge the findings challenge traditional models and note the study 'expands on several studies by these authors that are directed to determining the types and relative contributions of the components,' their request for 'more detailed, explicit discussion' about the role of PCF and 'clearer contrast with the dissociation of memory systems in the MB' suggests uncertainty about the broader theoretical conclusions regarding mammillary body function being independent of hippocampal inputs.
